events.text: An old farmer leans on your fence and watches you plant for a long time before saying anything. This is {npc}, who has grown spirit herbs in this valley since before you were born. "You are planting them like turnips," {he} says. "A spirit herb wants to see the morning first. Turn the bed east."

effects.log: You dig it again, east-facing. {npc} nods once, which, you learn later, is a great deal of praise from {him}.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what else you are doing wrong

effects.log: {npc} talks until dark. You understand a third of it. It is the most useful third you have ever heard.

choices.text: Thank {npc} and keep your turnip beds

effects.log: The herbs come up crooked and stubborn. {npc} brings you a cup of tea anyway.

events.text: The tenants of your fief stop work to watch their lord plant a spirit herb bed with bare hands. An old man among them, {npc}, finally walks over and kneels in the mud beside you. "If you are going to do it," {he} says, "do it properly. They will all copy you."

effects.log: By evening half the village is sowing spirit herbs the way {npc} does. Your fief smells of mint and wet earth.

choices.text: Work beside the tenants all day

effects.log: Nobody in the fief has seen a lord sweat before. They talk about it at every wedding for a year.

events.text: A soft year: rain at night, sun in the morning, and the herb beds so green they look painted. The bees are drunk on the flowers. Even the weeds seem to be trying their best.

effects.log: You walk them slowly, touching the leaves. It is the best kind of tired.
The neighbours come, admire, and go home to look at their own fields with new eyes.

events.text: The good year brings more than herbs: a pair of cranes nests at the edge of your field, and the old people of the village say that means a house will be lucky for ten years.

effects.log: You put a little fence around the nest. The cranes watch you build it as if they approve.
People walk out from three villages to see them. You sell nobody anything, and feel rich.

events.text: No rain for three months. The herb beds curl at the edges like old letters, and every evening you carry water from the well until your shoulders scream. It is not enough. It is never enough in a drought.

effects.log: You save what you can. Your hands blister and harden.

choices.text: Share your well with the village

effects.log: Your own beds suffer for it. Nobody in the village forgets who opened the gate.

events.text: The drought cracks the earth so wide you can put your hand in it. An old rainmaker comes through the valley selling prayers by the line. Everyone buys one. It rains the day after he leaves, which proves nothing at all.

effects.log: You stand in it until you are soaked. Some things do not need to be proved.

choices.text: Dig a deeper well for next time

effects.log: It takes a month. The next drought will find you ready.

events.text: The river comes over its banks in the night and takes half the herb beds with it. In the morning your fields are a brown lake with spirit herbs floating in it like lost hats.

choices.text: Wade in and save what you can

effects.log: You save a basket. The river keeps the rest, and one of your sandals.
Their houses are lower than your fields. By the time you get back there is nothing to save. You do not regret it.

events.text: Grey rot creeps across the herb beds overnight, leaf to leaf, until the whole field smells of wet ash. The old farmers say the blight comes once a generation, and this is it.

choices.text: Burn the beds and start clean

effects.log: The smoke hangs over the valley for a day. Next year the soil will be sweet again.

choices.text: Try to save the healthy rows

effects.log: You lose them anyway, one by one. You learn more about rot than you ever wanted to.

events.text: Little green beetles in their thousands, shining like spilled jade. They eat the herb beds from the edges in, and the untended rows go first.

choices.text: Pick them off by hand, all night

effects.log: You fill three jars. The chickens next door have the best week of their lives.

choices.text: Swear to tend the fields next year

effects.log: You swear it to the beetles, who are not listening.

events.text: An ordinary year in the fields: some rain, some sun, some weeds. The tended rows stand up straight; the herbs smell faintly of qi when you brush past them, like a room someone has just meditated in.

effects.log: You fall asleep under the willow and wake up with a leaf on your face.
You draw the beds in the dirt with a stick. Next year will be better. Next year always will be.

events.text: The year turns and the fields give what they give. You count the harvest twice, out of habit, and the old willow at the field's corner drops its leaves on the count.

choices.text: Bring a bundle to the village shrine

effects.log: You leave the first bundle at the shrine, as farmers do. Nobody sees. That is the point.
The count does not change. You feel better anyway.

events.text: Three years in the ground and the ginseng comes up shaped like a little sleeping person, roots for arms and legs. It smells of old forests. You lift it out as carefully as a newborn.

effects.log: You wrap it the way the old herbalists did. It goes into your bag like a treasure.
The neighbours gather around it in silence, as if it might wake up.

events.text: The Scarlet Vermilion Fruit ripens in a single night, and in the morning the whole field glows faintly red, as if a lantern had been left burning in the grass.

effects.log: It is warm in your hand, warmer than the sun can explain.

choices.text: Let the village children see it glow

effects.log: The children are silent for once. One of them asks if it is a star.

events.text: You grew a Snow Lotus in a field that has never seen snow. Four years of shade cloths, ice from the mountain, and worry. It opens one morning, white as a held breath, and the air around it is cold.

effects.log: Your lungs fill with mountain air. For a moment you are on a peak you have never climbed.

choices.text: Cut it with a silver knife

effects.log: The old way. The lotus goes into your bag still cold.

events.text: Footprints in the herb beds at dawn, small and quick, and half the harvest gone. Pinned to your fence with a hairpin is a note in terrible handwriting: SORRY. VERY HUNGRY. WILL PAY BACK. It is signed with a drawing of a magpie.

choices.text: Laugh, and leave a bowl of rice out

effects.log: The bowl is empty in the morning. Another note: THANK YOU. STILL SORRY.
You will keep a watch next year. The magpie, wherever it is, sleeps badly.

events.text: Your lantern catches a thin young man knee-deep in the herb beds, an armful of stolen leaves and a face of pure despair. "{npc}," {he} says, before you ask. "People call me Magpie. I am a very bad thief."

effects.log: {npc} stares at you, then at the herbs, then bursts into tears. You have a farmhand.
The magistrate thanks you. {npc} does not look back as they lead {him} away.
{npc} bows nine times and runs. You suspect you will see {him} again.

events.text: The magpie has been back. The herb beds are picked over with an expert's care, and on the fence is a single coin and a note: PAYING BACK. SLOWLY. It is not nearly enough. It is something.

effects.log: You put the coin on the windowsill. It becomes a sort of joke between you and someone you have never met.
Next year the lantern will be lit.

events.text: The province's alchemists send a cart for your herbs, and with it a young apprentice who sniffs every bundle like a wine taster. "These were grown east-facing," the apprentice says. "Who taught you that?"

effects.log: The apprentice writes it down. The old farmer will be famous in a furnace room somewhere.
You load it yourself. The carter tells everyone on the road who grows the best herbs.

events.text: Your sect's pill hall receives your harvest with the solemnity of a funeral and the joy of a wedding. The elder in charge of the furnaces, who has never once smiled at you, smiles.

effects.log: The elder bows back, which the younger disciples talk about for a week.

choices.text: Ask what the pills will be for

effects.log: "For the young ones," the elder says. "For the breakthroughs they are not ready for yet."

events.text: Ten years in the ground, and the Heaven-Root is a single leaf the colour of a dragonfly's wing. It has not grown in a year. Then, one morning, there are two.

effects.log: Two. You count them again anyway, every morning, for a month.
A tiny roof of tiles over a single plant. The neighbours think you have lost your mind. You may have.

events.text: Thirty years. The Heaven-Root stands knee-high now, and the soil around it is warm even in winter. Wild deer come to the fence at night and stand there, watching it, never eating. A stranger at the market asks, very casually, what you grow.

effects.log: The stranger smiles as if you had said something else entirely, and walks away.
The stranger buys a bundle of ordinary herbs and goes. You do not sleep well that night.

events.text: Fifty years. The Heaven-Root's leaves move when there is no wind, slowly, like something breathing. When you sit beside it your qi settles of its own accord, and the old pains of your life feel a long way off.

choices.text: Sit with it through a night

effects.log: You sit until dawn. In the morning you feel as if you had slept for a week.
You make the promise out loud. Something in the leaves seems to hear.

events.text: In the family garden, behind a little fence of tiles, grows a plant older than you are. Your parent tended it every day of their life. The old note tied to the fence says only: KEEP IT GROWING. IT IS ALMOST THERE.

effects.log: It is warm. You will keep it growing.

choices.text: Read every note your parent left

effects.log: There are dozens, in a box under the fence: weather, pests, worries, hope. You read them all.

events.text: The Heaven-Root dies the way old people do: slowly, then all at once. One morning its leaves are grey, and by evening it is only a dry stalk. Decades of work go back into the earth.

effects.log: You dig a proper grave for it at the field's edge. You are not ashamed of the tears.

choices.text: Save its seeds, if there are any

effects.log: There are none. You knew there would be none. You looked anyway.

events.text: In the dark three figures come over the wall with a spade and a jade box. Your lantern finds them first. The leader drops the spade and bows: "Madam Hwang Boyeon, the apothecary, sends her apologies. She also sends an offer."

choices.text: Refuse the offer and the apology

effects.log: They leave over the wall the way they came. Madam Hwang, they say, will try again in another way.

choices.text: Send them home with a cup of tea

effects.log: They drink it, bewildered, and go. You have made a strange kind of friend.

events.text: Someone has dug at the Heaven-Root in the night and been interrupted, or lost their nerve. The roots are torn on one side, and a jade box lies smashed in the grass. A name is stamped on the lid: Hwang.

choices.text: Bind the torn roots with moss

effects.log: You work until noon. It will live. It will remember.

choices.text: Go and see Madam Hwang Boyeon

effects.log: The apothecary receives you with perfect politeness and denies everything. You both know.

events.text: Sixty years. The Heaven-Root flowers at midnight, a single bloom as white as moonlight on snow, and the whole valley smells of it. In the morning the root is ready. Everyone who has ever wanted it knows, somehow, by noon.

choices.text: Stand guard over it all day

effects.log: You stand guard until the stars come out. Nobody comes. Nobody would dare.

choices.text: Sit beside it and remember the decades

effects.log: Every drought, every flood, every frightened night. It was worth all of them.

events.text: At a market a seed seller holds out a dry brown seed the size of a fingernail. "A Heaven-Root," the seller says. "Sixty years. Nobody has the patience any more." Your hand is already reaching for it.

effects.log: It is warm. Of course it is. You give it back, smiling, and do not know why.
"Long ago," the seller says. "Somebody who loved a field more than a fortune."
